questions.question: Each of the clerks ____ responsible for filing the reports on time.
questions.explanation: “Each” is singular, so it takes the singular verb “is,” regardless of the plural noun that follows.

questions.question: Neither the mayor nor the councilors ____ present at the hearing yesterday.
questions.explanation: With “neither…nor,” the verb agrees with the nearer subject (“councilors”), which is plural; the past-time marker “yesterday” calls for “were.”

questions.question: The group of employees ____ asked to submit their forms before noon.
questions.explanation: The subject is the singular “group,” not “employees,” so the singular past verb “was” is correct.

questions.question: She ____ the application form last Monday.
questions.explanation: The past-time phrase “last Monday” requires the simple past tense, “submitted.”

questions.question: If the office ____ earlier, we would have avoided the long queue.
questions.explanation: A third conditional (would have + past participle) uses the past perfect in the if-clause: “had opened.”

questions.question: The number of applicants ____ increased this year.
questions.explanation: “The number of” takes a singular verb, so “has increased” is correct (unlike “a number of,” which is plural).

questions.question: Ramon is the only one of the employees who ____ never been late.
questions.explanation: “Only one” is the antecedent of “who,” so the verb is singular: “has.”

questions.question: By the time the director arrived, the meeting ____ already started.
questions.explanation: An action completed before another past action uses the past perfect: “had already started.”

questions.question: Not only the supervisor but also the staff members ____ invited to the seminar.
questions.explanation: With “not only…but also,” the verb agrees with the nearer subject “staff members,” which is plural, so “were.”

questions.question: It is essential that every applicant ____ a valid ID on the day of the exam.
questions.explanation: After expressions of necessity such as “it is essential that,” the subjunctive uses the base verb: “bring.”

questions.question: Hardly ____ the report when the power went out.
questions.explanation: “Hardly” at the start of a sentence triggers inversion with the past perfect: “had she finished.”

questions.question: The committee, along with its advisers, ____ to meet next week.
questions.explanation: “Along with” phrases do not change the subject; the singular “committee” takes “is.”

questions.question: Had the clerk verified the documents, the error ____ avoided.
questions.explanation: “Had + past participle” is an inverted third conditional, so the result clause needs “would have been.”

questions.question: The mayor, as well as the barangay captains, ____ expected to sign the agreement.
questions.explanation: “As well as” does not make the subject plural; the singular “mayor” takes “is.”

questions.question: Economics ____ one of the subjects tested in the examination.
questions.explanation: Names of academic subjects ending in -ics (economics, mathematics) are singular, so “is.”

questions.question: The new policy will take effect ____ January 1.
questions.explanation: Use “on” with specific dates.

questions.question: She is very good ____ solving numerical problems.
questions.explanation: The fixed adjective phrase is “good at” for a skill.

questions.question: The office is closed ____ weekends and holidays.
questions.explanation: “On weekends” is the standard phrase for recurring days.

questions.question: The manager insisted ____ reviewing every file personally.
questions.explanation: The verb “insist” takes the preposition “on” (insist on doing something).

questions.question: The funds were divided ____ the three departments.
questions.explanation: “Among” is used for more than two parties; “between” is for two.

questions.question: He is allergic ____ seafood, so he avoided the buffet.
questions.explanation: The adjective “allergic” is followed by “to.”

questions.question: Please comply ____ the guidelines before submitting the form.
questions.explanation: “Comply” is followed by “with.”

questions.question: The committee is composed ____ five senior officers.
questions.explanation: “Composed of” is the correct phrase meaning made up of.

questions.question: She was appointed ____ the position of records officer last month.
questions.explanation: We are appointed “to” a position.

questions.question: The agency is accountable ____ the public for how it spends taxes.
questions.explanation: One is accountable “to” a person or group (and “for” a thing); the blank precedes “the public,” so “to.”

questions.question: The director took full responsibility ____ the delay.
questions.explanation: “Responsibility for” is the standard pairing.

questions.question: Veteran officials are often immune ____ criticism.
questions.explanation: “Immune” is followed by “to.”

questions.question: The audit report differs significantly ____ last year's findings.
questions.explanation: “Differ” takes “from” when comparing two things.

questions.question: The new rules are inconsistent ____ the existing code of conduct.
questions.explanation: “Inconsistent” is followed by “with.”

questions.question: He was prevented ____ attending the training by a sudden illness.
questions.explanation: “Prevent someone from doing something” is the correct construction.

questions.question: The employee gave a ____ reason for his absence, so the HR office excused him.
questions.explanation: “Valid” means acceptable and well-founded; the other choices do not describe a reason that would be excused.

questions.question: The new law will ____ the rights of workers in small businesses.
questions.explanation: “Protect” means to keep safe; it is the only option that makes sense with “rights of workers.”

questions.question: The weather bureau issued a ____ about the approaching typhoon.
questions.explanation: A “warning” is an alert about danger; “warrant” and “warranty” have legal or commercial meanings.

questions.question: The mayor's speech was so ____ that many in the audience were moved to tears.
questions.explanation: “Poignant” means deeply touching, which explains the tears.

questions.question: Because of the budget cuts, the agency must be ____ in its spending.
questions.explanation: “Frugal” means careful with money, which suits budget cuts; the others imply waste or carelessness.

questions.question: The witness gave a ____ account, leaving out no important detail.
questions.explanation: “Comprehensive” means complete and thorough, matching “leaving out no important detail.”

questions.question: The official's ____ remarks offended many members of the community.
questions.explanation: “Tactless” means lacking sensitivity, which explains why people were offended; the other options are positive or neutral.

questions.question: Her ____ to detail made her the best proofreader in the office.
questions.explanation: “Attention to detail” is the standard collocation, and it is the only positive choice that explains the praise.

questions.question: The board decided to ____ the old policy and replace it with a simpler one.
questions.explanation: “Revoke” means to officially cancel, which fits “replace it”; the others keep or strengthen the policy.

questions.question: The scandal had a ____ effect on public trust, damaging it for years.
questions.explanation: “Detrimental” means harmful, matching “damaging it for years.”

questions.question: The lawyer's argument was ____, leaving the jury with no room for doubt.
questions.explanation: “Cogent” means clear, logical and convincing, which leaves no room for doubt.

questions.question: The minister's ____ stance on corruption earned him the respect of both allies and critics.
questions.explanation: “Unwavering” means steady and firm, which would earn respect; “equivocal” and “capricious” suggest indecision.

questions.question: The auditor's report was a ____ of the agency's wasteful practices, naming every offense.
questions.explanation: An “indictment” is a strong accusation, fitting a report that names every offense.

questions.question: The two accounts of the incident were so ____ that investigators could not reconcile them.
questions.explanation: “Discrepant” means inconsistent; accounts that cannot be reconciled differ from each other.

questions.question: The treasurer's ____ handling of funds ensured that no money was ever misplaced.
questions.explanation: “Meticulous” means extremely careful, which explains why no money was misplaced.

questions.question: The road was flooded; ____, the employees could not report for work.
questions.explanation: “Therefore” signals a result: the flooding caused the absence.

questions.question: The exam was difficult. ____, most of the examinees passed.
questions.explanation: “Nevertheless” signals contrast: passing was unexpected given the difficulty.

questions.question: Maria studied every night; ____, she passed the exam with a high score.
questions.explanation: “As a result” introduces the consequence of studying every night.

questions.question: He wanted to attend the seminar ____ he had too much work.
questions.explanation: “But” links two contrasting ideas: wanting to attend and being unable to.

questions.question: The company must cut costs. ____, it plans to freeze hiring for six months.
questions.explanation: “To that end” means for that purpose, linking the plan to the goal of cutting costs.

questions.question: ____ the heavy rain, the ceremony proceeded as scheduled.
questions.explanation: “Despite” signals contrast; the other options introduce a cause, which does not fit the ceremony continuing.

questions.question: You will not receive your certificate ____ you complete all the requirements.
questions.explanation: “Unless” means “if not,” which expresses the required condition.

questions.question: The first proposal was too costly; ____, the second was affordable.
questions.explanation: “By contrast” signals the opposite relationship between the two proposals.

questions.question: Public servants are expected to be honest. ____, they must treat every citizen fairly.
questions.explanation: “Furthermore” adds a related expectation; the other options signal contrast or an alternative.

questions.question: The project was completed ahead of schedule, ____ the shortage of staff.
questions.explanation: Finishing early despite a shortage is contrast, so “in spite of” is needed; the others imply cause.

questions.question: ____ the new system is faster, many employees still prefer the old one.
questions.explanation: “Although” introduces a concession that contrasts with the main clause.

questions.question: Submit your requirements today; ____, your application will not be processed.
questions.explanation: “Otherwise” means “if you do not,” stating the consequence of failing to submit.

questions.question: The data seemed to support the hypothesis. ____, a closer analysis revealed serious errors in how it was collected.
questions.explanation: “However” marks the contrast between the apparent support and the flaws that were later found.

questions.question: The mayor is neither corrupt ____ incompetent.
questions.explanation: “Neither” is paired with “nor.”

questions.question: Employees were told to arrive early; ____ the director's arrival was delayed until noon.
questions.explanation: “Ironically” fits the unexpected outcome that the director himself was late; the others imply cause or addition.
